beats.narration_text: Hear 'Claude has an earnings-preview skill' and your brain fills in the rest — Claude is reading the numbers, forming a view, calling buy or sell. That's the natural inference. It's wrong.

Here's what's actually happening. Delete the skill's folder and Claude loses zero investment opinions — there were none to lose. The only thing that disappears is the ability to fill in that one template.

Open the folder. There's a license, and two files that do the work: a forty-four-page report template — the shape of the output — and a SKILL.md that tells Claude the four moves: pull the earnings transcript, map the competitors, note the valuation, fold in recent news.

Here's the mechanism. Claude reads SKILL.md, walks the four steps in the order the file specifies — transcript, competitors, valuation, news — and pours each result into the matching slot. No branching unless the file asks for it.

So the skill is a template-filler, not a stock picker. They optimized for consistency — same four-to-five page shape, same categories of fact, every run. The trade-off: Claude never volunteers an opinion the template didn't ask for.

Back to the two files. earnings-preview-single never handed Claude a view on the stock. What it guarantees: every run pulls the same four categories — transcript, competitors, valuation, news — into the same report-template shape. That's the entire promise.

beats.narration_text: Two things this reveals about reading the output. A number stated with total confidence doesn't prove Claude verified it against a second source — the template may simply present figures in a confident voice. A hedged claim doesn't prove the data was shaky — the template may ask for cautious language in that section regardless. Confidence and hedging are stylistic slots, not signals.

A skill called earnings-preview-single doesn't hand Claude a view on the stock. It's a template Claude fills in from the same categories of fact every run, and forming the actual investment opinion is still on you.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into any frontier LLM. It asks the model to map the skill before running it — which categories of fact get pulled, where each one lands in the template, and where the skill takes a position versus stays neutral. Then go deeper: design a skill for a domain you actually know, and mark where human judgment still lives.

llm_exercise.prompt: I want to understand what an 'agent skill' actually does before I trust its output. Read the earnings-preview-single skill on Anthropic's skills repo — the one that walks four categories of fact (earnings transcript, competitor landscape, valuation, recent news) into a four-to-five page report template. Before executing anything, walk me through: (1) which categories of fact the SKILL.md pulls, (2) which section of the report gets filled from which source, (3) where the skill takes a position versus where it stays neutral, and (4) which sentences in the finished report will be Claude's judgment versus which will be the template's fixed language. Don't write the report — produce the pre-flight map.
llm_exercise.dig_deeper: Go deeper: pick a domain you actually know — medicine, law, a hobby — and design a skill of your own. One report-template.md, one SKILL.md, three to five categories of fact. Where would you set the boundary between what the template asks for and what a human still has to judge?
